newsitem.title: USA: Consumer credit growth slows in February.
newsitem.headline: Consumer credit growth slows in February.

text.p: Consumers dug themselves into debt in February at a somewhat less vigorous pace than in January, but borrowing still exceeded the rate for the last half of 1996, the Federal Reserve Board said Monday.

Overall growth of consumer instalment credit, which includes all consumer borrowings except mortgages, slowed to $6.7 billion, or a seasonally adjusted 6.7 percent annual rate, in February, the Fed said.
In January, consumers added $10.2 billion to their debt burden, the most since last summer, lifting their borrowing pace to a 10.3 percent annual rate, it said.
Borrowing in February still outpaced the $5.3 billion-a-month average for the last half of 1996, but it was somewhat slower than the $7.46 billion monthly average for all of 1996, it said.
Consumer debt is reaching high levels, growing more sharply in 1996 than either personal income or consumer spending.

February's moderating, though still brisk, pace of borrowing comes amid relatively high levels of consumer confidence during a month in which consumers decided to save more of their gains in personal income and slow their spending growth.

Credit card buying, or revolving debt, which fuelled the surge in indebtedness in January, grew at a less frantic pace in February. Credit-card debt rose by $5.1 billion in February at a 12.7 percent annual rate, down from January's 16-month high $8.4 billion gain at a 21.6 percent rate, the Fed said.
The Fed said loans to buy new cars were almost unchanged in February, expanding at a scant 0.3 percent annual rate, after growing by $1 billion at a 3.1 percent rate in January, it said.

So-called other credit, a catch-all category that includes borrowings such as loans for education or to buy boats or trailers, rose by $1.6 billion in February at a 5.5 percent annual rate, after rising by $800 million in January at a 2.9 percent annual rate.
